messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Questions About Large Differences Between DIC and WAIC
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Questions About Large Differences Between DIC and WAIC
messages.body_plain:
DIC and WAIC are different and does not always agree, although they usually do.

WAIC has a better (Bayesian) justification and is to be preferred

if the results are very sensitive, it can be some issues with data, or rather a
data/model conflict

with DIC/WAIC then only relative numbers makes sense, so comparing absolute
numbers is less meaningful.

You might chose to use CPO instead, or better, the group-version of it, see
vignette in the R-INLA package.

On Wed, 2024-11-27 at 04:57 -0800, Javier martin wrote:
>  Hello everyone,
>
> I am a new user on the forum and I am just starting to use INLA. I am working
> on spatiotemporal models and I have a question that I hope you can help me
> solve.
>
> I am currently fitting spatiotemporal models with interaction random effects
> following the Knorr-Held scheme, that is, using the Kronecker product to
> combine the spatial and temporal effect structure matrices (types I, II, III
> or IV). My idea is to fit models with various structures for both interaction
> effects and direct effects of time (iid, RW1, RW2) and space (LCAR, ICAR,
> etc.), comparing them using fit measures such as DIC and WAIC, and also using
> predictive measures such as CPO.
>
> When comparing the models, I expected to find close values ​​between DIC and
> WAIC, since both are based on model likelihood, with slight differences
> arising from their definitions. However, I have been surprised to find very
> large differences in several models, on the order of 10^3. This makes model
> selection difficult and makes me wonder if I am making a mistake in the model
> specification or violating one of its assumptions.
>
> On the forum I found a comment that said:
> "However, sometimes you get a massive difference in DIC or WAIC, like 10000.
> That gives you a strong hint that one of the models are better."
> However, I would like to understand more in depth why these differences occur
> and how to interpret them.
>
> To give more context, I'm sharing an example of the code I'm using to fit the
> models in INLA:
>
> sdunif = "expression:
> logdens=-log_precision/2;
> return(logdens)"
>
> lunif = "expression:
> a = 1;
> b = 1;
> beta = exp(theta)/(1+exp(theta));
> logdens = lgamma(a+b)-lgamma(a)-lgamma(b)+(a-1)*log(beta)+(b-1)*log(1-beta);
> log_jacobian = log(beta*(1-beta));
> return(logdens+log_jacobian)"
>
> g <- inla.read.graph("...")
>
> Qs <- matrix(0, g$n, g$n)
> for (i in 1:g$n) {
>  Qs[i, i] = g$nnbs[[i]]
>  Qs[i, g$nbs[[i]]] = -1
> }
> R.Leroux <- diag(dim(Qs)[1]) - Qs
>
> mod.st0 <- inla(O ~ f(ID_muni, model = "generic1", Cmatrix = R.Leroux, constr
> = TRUE,
>  hyper = list(prec = list(prior = sdunif), beta = list(prior = lunif, initial
> = 0))) +
>  f(ID_year, model = "iid", constr = TRUE,
>  hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01)))),
>  family = "poisson", data = Data_sp, E = E,
>  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, cdf = c(log(1))),
>  control.fixed = list(mean.intercept = 0, prec.intercept = 0.001),
>  control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE),
>  control.inla = list(strategy = "simplified.laplace"),
>  num.threads = 4)
>
> Results obtained for this model:
>
> Specifically, with this model you obtain:
> Deviance Information Criterion (DIC)...............: 12481.61
> Deviance Information Criterion (DIC, saturated) ....: 4186.50
> Effective number of parameters .....................: -758.54
>
> Watanabe-Akaike information criterion (WAIC) ...: 14445.87
> Effective number of parameters.................: 667.39
>
> Marginal log-Likelihood: -7648.46
>
> I would really appreciate any explanation about these differences.
>
> Thanks in advance to everyone and best regards.
> Javier

Many thanks,
Erin

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Space-time model covariate
messages.body_plain:
This depends on whether the covariate has an instantaneous effect (in which case the finer resolution is only useful for interpolation/prediction) or some kind of aggregate effect (in which case one might be able to build a model for how it links to the observations). So one would need to understand the mechanisms behind the observations to be able to give an appropriate answer in any particular model/data case.
Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA users,

In my computation when I fix the hyperparameters precision (log precision), INLA takes a long time to converge. Can you tell me what can be a possible reason? I write a snippet of code.

PS: I have a 15 random effect spatially varying coefficients. As INLA takes a long time to converge if I do not fix i am putting some initial value. Smaller precision sometime helps. But with an example of big data, without fixing the hyperparameters I got the initial guess.

f(as.numeric(spatial_ID_13),value_r1__value_u1,
                               constr=FALSE,
                               model = "besag",scale.model=TRUE,
                               graph = graph_adjacency_2,
                               hyper=list(theta = list(prior = "loggamma",
                                                       param=c(1,.0003),
                                                      initial=log(5.0),
                                                      fixed=TRUE,
                                                      scale.model=TRUE)
                               )
                              )

The other alignment is

```
 family = "poisson" ,

                            data = data.frame(x_matrix_2) ,

                            control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
                            control.compute = list(openmp.strategy = "huge",
                                                   dic = TRUE,config = TRUE,
                                                   save.memory = TRUE),
                            control.inla = list(
                              #diagonal = .01,
                              strategy="gaussian",
                              int.strategy = "eb"
                              ),
                            #verbose=TRUE,

                            control.mode=list(restart=T)
```

Is the diagonal term added to the Kronecker product of Q_spde and Q_rw1_scaled? After adding the diagonal term, does INLA rescale the combined precision matrix to make the generalized variance = 1?

Thanks,
Ruby

messages.body_plain:
Hi Haavard,

I came across a new question related to the RW1 model. The precision is a hyperparameter in the model: f(year, model="rw1", scale.model=TRUE).

The precision matrix, Q, is defined as precision * R, where R is the structure matrix reflecting the neighborhood structure of the model.

I scaled Q using inla.scale.model(Q, constr = list(A = matrix(1, 1, n), e = 0)) and noticed that, regardless of the precision value, the scaled Q (Q.scaled) remains the same. If this is the case, how is the precision estimated?

Thanks,

Ruby

Thank you very much for your explanation. I will use the group-version of the CPO and consider the WAIC as an alternative.

Thank you again for your help.

El lunes, 2 de diciembre de 2024 a las 8:46:45 UTC+1, Helpdesk (Haavard Rue) escribió:
>
> DIC and WAIC are different and does not always agree, although they usually do.
>
> WAIC has a better (Bayesian) justification and is to be preferred
>
> if the results are very sensitive, it can be some issues with data, or rather a
> data/model conflict
>
>
> with DIC/WAIC then only relative numbers makes sense, so comparing absolute
> numbers is less meaningful.
>
> You might chose to use CPO instead, or better, the group-version of it, see
> vignette in the R-INLA package.
>
>
>
>
>
> On Wed, 2024-11-27 at 04:57 -0800, Javier martin wrote:
> >  Hello everyone,
> >
> > I am a new user on the forum and I am just starting to use INLA. I am working
> > on spatiotemporal models and I have a question that I hope you can help me
> > solve.
> >
> > I am currently fitting spatiotemporal models with interaction random effects
> > following the Knorr-Held scheme, that is, using the Kronecker product to
> > combine the spatial and temporal effect structure matrices (types I, II, III
> > or IV). My idea is to fit models with various structures for both interaction
> > effects and direct effects of time (iid, RW1, RW2) and space (LCAR, ICAR,
> > etc.), comparing them using fit measures such as DIC and WAIC, and also using
> > predictive measures such as CPO.
> >
> > When comparing the models, I expected to find close values ​​between DIC and
> > WAIC, since both are based on model likelihood, with slight differences
> > arising from their definitions. However, I have been surprised to find very
> > large differences in several models, on the order of 10^3. This makes model
> > selection difficult and makes me wonder if I am making a mistake in the model
> > specification or violating one of its assumptions.
> >
> > On the forum I found a comment that said:
> > "However, sometimes you get a massive difference in DIC or WAIC, like 10000.
> > That gives you a strong hint that one of the models are better."
> > However, I would like to understand more in depth why these differences occur
> > and how to interpret them.
> >
> > To give more context, I'm sharing an example of the code I'm using to fit the
> > models in INLA:
> >
> > sdunif = "expression:
> > logdens=-log_precision/2;
> > return(logdens)"
> >
> > lunif = "expression:
> > a = 1;
> > b = 1;
> > beta = exp(theta)/(1+exp(theta));
> > logdens = lgamma(a+b)-lgamma(a)-lgamma(b)+(a-1)*log(beta)+(b-1)*log(1-beta);
> > log_jacobian = log(beta*(1-beta));
> > return(logdens+log_jacobian)"
> >
> > g <- inla.read.graph("...")
> >
> > Qs <- matrix(0, g$n, g$n)
> > for (i in 1:g$n) {
> >  Qs[i, i] = g$nnbs[[i]]
> >  Qs[i, g$nbs[[i]]] = -1
> > }
> > R.Leroux <- diag(dim(Qs)[1]) - Qs
> >
> > mod.st0 <- inla(O ~ f(ID_muni, model = "generic1", Cmatrix = R.Leroux, constr
> > = TRUE,
> >  hyper = list(prec = list(prior = sdunif), beta = list(prior = lunif, initial
> > = 0))) +
> >  f(ID_year, model = "iid", constr = TRUE,
> >  hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01)))),
> >  family = "poisson", data = Data_sp, E = E,
> >  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, cdf = c(log(1))),
> >  control.fixed = list(mean.intercept = 0, prec.intercept = 0.001),
> >  control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE),
> >  control.inla = list(strategy = "simplified.laplace"),
> >  num.threads = 4)
> >
> > Results obtained for this model:
> >
> > Specifically, with this model you obtain:
> > Deviance Information Criterion (DIC)...............: 12481.61
> > Deviance Information Criterion (DIC, saturated) ....: 4186.50
> > Effective number of parameters .....................: -758.54
> >
> > Watanabe-Akaike information criterion (WAIC) ...: 14445.87
> > Effective number of parameters.................: 667.39
> >
> > Marginal log-Likelihood: -7648.46
> >
> > I would really appreciate any explanation about these differences.
> >
> > Thanks in advance to everyone and best regards.
> > Javier

Again, it depends on the mechanism, and how realistic a model you’re trying to make. The simplest model would just average the covariate across the observation gap, but that might be completely the wrong mechanism. This is a modelling and/or research question; I may be able to answer questions about how to implement a specific such model, but it’s really up to you to figure out what model it is you need/want.
Finn

Is it the instantaneous value on each 12th day, or is it the average across a 12 day long period, or is it something else? And what does it mean for a covariate to be available on that scale and another available on a daily scale? It sounds like it’s not the daily time scale covariate that’s the issue here, but rather how the _other_ covariates and the observations themselves behave. (The observations, a covariate “on the same timescale” and the daily scale covariate should be sufficient to show the principle)
Finn

messages.body_plain:
Details of f(z) needed. Linear combinations? Doable, either with
inlabru (bru_mapper_matrix in combination with any random effect model
on 1:12) or plain inla (some messy inla.stack call presumably; inlabru
much easier to achieve the same thing. Or perhaps f(..., A.local=...)
but I'm not sure) Some parametric non-linear function? etc, etc, etc,
etc.
The number of models that can be implemented is virtually infinite,
and explaining all of them, or even list a subset would take too much
time.
Software can help you implement models, but can't tell you which model
might in principle be worth considering (until after you've tried
them).
You need to provide the specifics of the model you wish to implement.
What such a model might look like is a research question specific to
your context, and not a software question.

Finn

messages.subject: Priors on AR(1) in spatio temporal model
messages.subject_clean: Priors on AR(1) in spatio temporal model
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have a spatio-temporal model for different rain scenarios.

I fit Rain_mean with a gamma distribution
Rain_max with a bgev distribution
and Dry_spells with a negative binomial distribution

the formula is given by
e.g. Rain_mean~ -1+Intercept+Latitude+Longitude+Elevation+f(field, model=spde.nonstat, group=field.group, control.group=list(model="ar1"))

the parameter estimate for the temporal correlation coefficient is for each scenario in the interval 0,93-0,99 which as far as I know is too high and indicates a non-stationary process

Would you add pc.priors in order to avoid overfitting?

Or would you change to a RW1 process? (I tried but it does not work, maybe I need priors too but I do not know which one to implement)

Can you maybe give me an advice on how to solve that problem or do you think these high temporal correlations can be argued somehow?

Very much looking forward to your answer.
Best,
Corinna

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Priors on AR(1) in spatio temporal model
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Priors on AR(1) in spatio temporal model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

1) high temporal correlation in the model described is expected when
you don't have anything else in the model to capture persistent
spatial structure; if your analysis domain is large enough,
long+lat+elev won't be enough for that.
The spatio-temporal process is then forced to deal with that, and the
only way to do that is to have a large temporal correlation. Adding a
purely spatial component may solve this problem (but also induces some
confounding between the components; whether this is a problem or not
depends on the amount of data etc).
2) A high AR(1) coefficient is interpretable as non-stationarity in
name only, and depends on how the limit is taken; in the inla "ar1"
model, the process model is always stationary, and rho-->1 leads to a
temporally _constant_ model, in the form of a single random variable
with variance given by the model.

Note that this is different from the intrinsic-stationary rw1 model,
that by default has a sum-to-zero constraint, and scale.model=TRUE
rescales the average variance. The effect of imposing the constraint
results in a truly nonstationary model. However, without the
constraint, the model is intrinsic-stationary (the first order
differences are stationary). Some literature calls that a
non-stationary model because of the Brownian motion anchored at B(0)=0
is a truly non-stationary process, but when used as a random walk, the
nonstationarity concept isn't really the right way to think about it,
as it mostly behaves a a stationary process, just with infinite
correlation range and large overall variance.
When the issue leading to a large AR coefficient is that there are
unmodeled spatially persistent effects in the data, then applying a
random walk doesn't solve problem at all, as it's not constructed to
be persistent! (and when constrained to sum to zero ight even make
things worse).

One thing to check is what happens if you remove the time aspect of
the model entirely, and just have a spatial component. If that
component has spatial structure, you likely need it in the model even
when you add time.

In some case, one can get away with the joint space-time component
capturing everything, but not always.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Say I have Gaussian data where the independent noise parameter differs by (assumed known) groups but with the same latent field. My data is spatial but to illustrate it visually see the first plot in 1D.
ie assume we have
Y_g1 ~ U + N(0,(sigma_g1)^2)
Y_g2 ~ U + N(0,(sigma_g2)^2)

eg in this example sigma_g1 = 0.05 and sigma_g2 = 0.3

In essence I have a spatial process that may be measured in two ways, each with an associated error. (Or potentially up to say 3/4 groups). Can such a model be fit with inla , assume the general structure of my code is as follows (Taken from a worked example in E. T. Krainski et al. (2019)).

spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern( ... ) # mesh/priors for range/ std dev

formula <- response ~ -1 + beta0 + f(i, model = spde) # may also include covaraites

data_stack<- inla.stack(
  data = list(response =  df$response),
  A = list(A5, 1),
  effects = list(i = 1:spde$n.spde,
    beta0 = rep(1, nrow(df))),
  tag = 'est')

res5 <- inla(formula,
  data = inla.stack.data(data_stack),
  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A( data_stack  )))

and assume some df contains the data:  X ,Y , Group , response.

Additionally if the above is possible, can I then assume priors could be placed on them (ie if prior knowledge is that g1 should have high precision and g2 should have low precision)

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
One option is to include a separate random effect for each group to account for this. If your observation model i Gaussin (like your toy example) that would however make those variances mutually nonidentifiable with the inla observation model variance. To handle that, you could set the observation model precision to a fixed, large value, in effect trading the observations as near-exact, given the random effects.

But I think there may also be a special model that allows a few fixed effects in the precision model; some binary indicators would then handle it.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA experts,

I have developed a model that considers the effect of "y" on "e". The model formula is as follows:

form <- y ~ -1 + y.b0 + e.b0 +

  f(year.y, model="rw1", scale.model=TRUE, constr=TRUE) +
  f(sy, model=spde) +

  f(year.e, model="rw1", scale.model=TRUE, constr=TRUE) +
  f(se, model=spde) +
  f(year.ey, copy="year.y", fixed=FALSE) +
  f(sey, copy="sy", same.as <http://same.as>="year.ey", fixed=FALSE)

Now, I want to explore the lagged effect of "y" on "e". That means, I am interested in determining whether "y" from the previous year could impact "e" in the current year. Is it possible to model this effect?

Thanks,
Ruby

While seeing the optimiser trace might be useful for internal debugging, I don’t think it would be of general use (optimisers don’t necessarily take an humanly logical path towards the optimum) and the amount of data storage would be huge, as would the added time of actually writing all those values to disk; storing hundreds of copies of the model would be really bad. That said, nonlinear inlabru models do store the trace (usually the number of iterations is small, so the memory requirement is less than it would be to store the full inla optimisation) of its iterated inla method for nonlinear predictor models; bru_convergence_plot() displays a summary (in light of my comments above I’ll likely at least make it an option to only store the convergence summaries).
Finn

> be huge, as would the added time of actually writing all those values to disk;
> storing hundreds of copies of the model would be really bad. That said,

> inla optimisation) of its iterated inla method for nonlinear predictor models;

messages.body_plain:
Hello INLA group.

I fitted a joint model (Binomial and weibull survival model) with some association structures and some log Conditional predictive ordinates (LCPO) are negative, like table below:

 I expected to find LCPO positive and close values between DIC and WAIC. I have been surprised to find very large differences in several models.
Someone has idea where is the mistake? For example, below the code to model III is:

m3 <- INLAjoint::joint(
                     formLong = list(Y2 ~ age + weekend + gender + (1  | ID_hosp) #GLMM
                    ),
    formSurv = inla.surv(time = I(los/365.25), event = Y1) ~ gender + age +  weekend, # survival
    dataLong = data,
    dataSurv = data,
    id = "ID_hosp",
    timeVar = "",
    corLong = FALSE,
    family = "binomial",
    basRisk = "weibullsurv",
    assoc = c("SRE"),
    control = list(int.strategy="eb",dic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE)
)

messages.body_plain:
As far as I know, no. But one can define scores in both direction.
check by comparing with the calculated individual cpo values…
However, for discrete data, lcpo should either all be negative or all positive, depending on the definition of the aggregated score. For continuous data it’s the log of a density, so can be both positive and negative with either definition…

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Negative LCPO
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Negative LCPO
messages.body_plain:
Hi Felipe,

To complete Finn's answer and in the specific context of your joint model, in order to account for the time-dependent linear combination of random effects in the survival submodel, we use some fake data that computes this linear combination to share. By default, INLA will include this fake data in the computation of dic, cpo and waic. You want to remove this part by only looking at values that corresponds to your longitudinal and survival submodels. For example for cpo:

CPO_l <- sum(m3$cpo$cpo[which(!is.na <http://is.na>(m3$.args$data$Yjoint[[1]]))]) # cpo longitudinal part
CPO_s <- sum(m3$cpo$cpo[which(!is.na <http://is.na>(m3$.args$data$Yjoint[[3]]))]) # cpo survival part
CPO_t <- CPO_l + CPO_s # cpo total

When you use "SRE_ind" instead of "SRE", the random effects are just copied and scaled (without the use of fake data) but this cannot be used to share anything time-dependent.

Best,
Denis

messages.subject: Spatial modeling of areal data
messages.subject_clean: Spatial modeling of areal data
messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA group,

I want  to estimate mortality rate or prevalence rate (crude rate) using the R-INLA package to produce smoothed county level mortality rate or prevalence rate (crude rate),  the model includes two random effects(spatially structured and unstructured random effect), and I assume the response variable Y(mortality rate) is lognormal distributed, how can I modify the code below:

Neighborhood matrix
#We create the neighborhood matrix needed to define the spatial random effect using the poly2nb() and the nb2INLA() functions
nb <- poly2nb(MapData_368version)
nb2INLA("map.adj", nb)

g <- inla.read.graph(filename = "map.adj")
#g which we will later use to specific the spatial random effect

Inference using INLA
#The model includes two random effects, for modeling the spatial residual variation, and modeling unstructured noise. We need to include two vectors in the data that denote the indices of these random effects. We call re_u the indices vector and re_v the indices vector. We set both re_u and re_v  equal to 1,...n is the number of counties. This can be obtained with the number of rows in the data (nrow(map)).
map$re_u  <- 1:nrow(map)
map$re_v  <- 1:nrow(map)

The response variable is Y. Random effects are defined using f() <https://rdrr.io/pkg/INLA/man/f.html> with parameters equal to the name of the index variable and the chosen model.  We use model = "besag" with neighborhood matrix given by g. We also use option scale.model = TRUE to make the precision parameter of models with different CAR priors comparable (Freni-Sterrantino, Ventrucci, and Rue 2018 <https://www.paulamoraga.com/book-geospatial/references.html#ref-FreniSterrantinoetal18>). Then, we choose model = "iid".
formula <- CrudeR ~ f(re_u, model = "besag", graph = g, scale.model = TRUE) + f(re_v, model = "iid")

We fit the model by calling the inla() <https://rdrr.io/pkg/INLA/man/inla.html> function. We specify the formula, family ("lognormal"), data. We also set control.predictor equal to list(compute = TRUE) to compute the posteriors of the predictions.
res <- inla(formula, family = "lognormal", data = map,
              control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
              control.compute = list(dic = TRUE))

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Determining covariate posteriors under fixed model
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Determining covariate posteriors under fixed model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Louis,

this is where linear model shorthand breaks down a bit, as it
conflates the values of a covariate with the _effect_ of the
covariate.
I _think_ what you want is the following model:

y[i] ~ exp(beta1*x1[i]) + beta2 * (x1[i] * x2[i])

where x1 and x2 are known numerical vectors where beta1 and beta2 are
unknown coefficients with Gaussian priors, and

y[i] ~ exp(beta1*x1[i]) + sum_k beta2[k] * x12[k]

if x2 is a factor variable, and x12 is whatever model.matrix()
constructs for the x1:x2 notation.

Then you can write this model with inlabru, in several ways:

Option 1, combined component effects:
  comp <- ~ 0 + x1(x1) + x12(~ 0 + x1:x2, model = "fixed")
  formula <- y ~ exp(x1) + x12
  fit <- bru(comp, bru_obs(formula, data = data.frame(x1=...,x2=...,y=...)))

In the predictor formula, x1 and x12 are the _effects of_ the
component definitions, i.e. beta1*x1[i] etc.
This also works if x1 or x2 are factor variables.
If both are numeric, the x12 component can be written x12(x1*x2) instead.

Option 2, explicit variables:
  comp <- ~ 0 + beta1(rep(1, nrow(.data.))) + beta2(rep(1, nrow(.data.)))
  formula <- y ~ exp(beta1 * x1) + beta2 * x1 *x2
  fit <- bru(comp, bru_obs(formula, data = data.frame(x1=...,x2=...,y=...)))

(in the case x1 and x2 are numeric covariates)

In your case, I'd probably go with Option 1.

If you don't have the latest inlabru, use like() instead of bru_obs().

Finn

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Determining covariate posteriors under fixed model
messages.body_plain:
Thank you for your answer, but I have probably asked incorrectly, and currently it seems to work with:

formula <- y ~ exp(x1) + x1x2
comp <- ~ 0 + x1(1) + x2(1)
fit <- bru(comp, bru_obs(formula, family="gaussian", data=data))

But now I'm facing a new problem. How do I specify priors on x1 and x2? I'm guessing it would involve using two linear components, but I couldn't find such an example of using multiple components.

On Tuesday, December 17, 2024 at 9:10:46 PM UTC+13 Finn Lindgren wrote:
> Hi Louis,
>
> this is where linear model shorthand breaks down a bit, as it
> conflates the values of a covariate with the _effect_ of the
> covariate.
> I _think_ what you want is the following model:
>
> y[i] ~ exp(beta1*x1[i]) + beta2 * (x1[i] * x2[i])
>
> where x1 and x2 are known numerical vectors where beta1 and beta2 are
> unknown coefficients with Gaussian priors, and
>
> y[i] ~ exp(beta1*x1[i]) + sum_k beta2[k] * x12[k]
>
> if x2 is a factor variable, and x12 is whatever model.matrix()
> constructs for the x1:x2 notation.
>
> Then you can write this model with inlabru, in several ways:
>
> Option 1, combined component effects:
> comp <- ~ 0 + x1(x1) + x12(~ 0 + x1:x2, model = "fixed")
> formula <- y ~ exp(x1) + x12
> fit <- bru(comp, bru_obs(formula, data = data.frame(x1=...,x2=...,y=...)))
>
> In the predictor formula, x1 and x12 are the _effects of_ the
> component definitions, i.e. beta1*x1[i] etc.
> This also works if x1 or x2 are factor variables.
> If both are numeric, the x12 component can be written x12(x1*x2) instead.
>
> Option 2, explicit variables:
> comp <- ~ 0 + beta1(rep(1, nrow(.data.))) + beta2(rep(1, nrow(.data.)))
> formula <- y ~ exp(beta1 * x1) + beta2 * x1 *x2
> fit <- bru(comp, bru_obs(formula, data = data.frame(x1=...,x2=...,y=...)))
>
> (in the case x1 and x2 are numeric covariates)
>
> In your case, I'd probably go with Option 1.
>
> If you don't have the latest inlabru, use like() instead of bru_obs().
>
> Finn
>
> On Tue, 17 Dec 2024 at 04:44, Louis Li <cooki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Dear INLA experts,
> >
> > Suppose I have covariates x1, x2 (gaussian priors) and a model y ~ exp(x1) + x1:x2, and I want the marginal posterior densities of x1 and x2.
> >
> > Is it possible to do in INLA or inlabru? Also how can I make R keep the coefficients of these two terms as 1, and have R recognize x1 and x2 as covariates instead of exp(x1) and x1:x2?
> >
> > Thanks in advance.
> > Louis

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for answering.
I think I kind of locate the source of the error In my code

base.formula <- Incidence_mod ~ 1 +

  f(ID.City, model = "bym2", replicate = year, graph = W.City, scale.model = TRUE, diagonal=1e-4) +
  f(month, replicate = ID.City, model = "rw1", cyclic = TRUE, constr = TRUE, scale.model = TRUE, diagonal=1e-4)
I found the problem is in my spatial variable.
When I delete the marked part (replicate = year), the model processes just fine.
I am not really familiar with this method and I suppose that part allows the difference within different years maybe?
So how can I solve the problem? Thank you again.

messages.body_plain:
That model doesn’t have any covariates, just two scalar variables x1 and x2.
Since those are by default model=“linear”, you can set their prior mean and precision with

comp <- 0+x1(1, mean.linear=…, prec.linear=…) + x2(…1)

But since the predictor expression will also become a scalar, you may still need to use the rep(1, nrow(.data.)) as input to x1 and x2 to help inlabru figure out the appropriate size of the predictor.

Btw, I assume you meant exp(x1) + x1 * x2 in the predictor.

Finn

> On 18 Dec 2024, at 00:26, Louis Li <cooki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ﻿

> Thank you for your answer, but I have probably asked incorrectly, and currently it seems to work with:
>
> formula <- y ~ exp(x1) + x1x2
> comp <- ~ 0 + x1(1) + x2(1)
> fit <- bru(comp, bru_obs(formula, family="gaussian", data=data))
>
> But now I'm facing a new problem. How do I specify priors on x1 and x2? I'm guessing it would involve using two linear components, but I couldn't find such an example of using multiple components.
>
>
> On Tuesday, December 17, 2024 at 9:10:46 PM UTC+13 Finn Lindgren wrote:
> > Hi Louis,
> >
> > this is where linear model shorthand breaks down a bit, as it
> > conflates the values of a covariate with the _effect_ of the
> > covariate.
> > I _think_ what you want is the following model:
> >
> > y[i] ~ exp(beta1*x1[i]) + beta2 * (x1[i] * x2[i])
> >
> > where x1 and x2 are known numerical vectors where beta1 and beta2 are
> > unknown coefficients with Gaussian priors, and
> >
> > y[i] ~ exp(beta1*x1[i]) + sum_k beta2[k] * x12[k]
> >
> > if x2 is a factor variable, and x12 is whatever model.matrix()
> > constructs for the x1:x2 notation.
> >
> > Then you can write this model with inlabru, in several ways:
> >
> > Option 1, combined component effects:
> > comp <- ~ 0 + x1(x1) + x12(~ 0 + x1:x2, model = "fixed")
> > formula <- y ~ exp(x1) + x12
> > fit <- bru(comp, bru_obs(formula, data = data.frame(x1=...,x2=...,y=...)))
> >
> > In the predictor formula, x1 and x12 are the _effects of_ the
> > component definitions, i.e. beta1*x1[i] etc.
> > This also works if x1 or x2 are factor variables.
> > If both are numeric, the x12 component can be written x12(x1*x2) instead.
> >
> > Option 2, explicit variables:
> > comp <- ~ 0 + beta1(rep(1, nrow(.data.))) + beta2(rep(1, nrow(.data.)))
> > formula <- y ~ exp(beta1 * x1) + beta2 * x1 *x2
> > fit <- bru(comp, bru_obs(formula, data = data.frame(x1=...,x2=...,y=...)))
> >
> > (in the case x1 and x2 are numeric covariates)
> >
> > In your case, I'd probably go with Option 1.
> >
> > If you don't have the latest inlabru, use like() instead of bru_obs().
> >
> > Finn
> >
> > On Tue, 17 Dec 2024 at 04:44, Louis Li <cooki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Dear INLA experts,
> > >
> > > Suppose I have covariates x1, x2 (gaussian priors) and a model y ~ exp(x1) + x1:x2, and I want the marginal posterior densities of x1 and x2.
> > >
> > > Is it possible to do in INLA or inlabru? Also how can I make R keep the coefficients of these two terms as 1, and have R recognize x1 and x2 as covariates instead of exp(x1) and x1:x2?
> > >
> > > Thanks in advance.
> > > Louis

messages.body_plain:
1. Check that your year values are integers taking values 1,2,3,etc and not actual years.
2. Perhaps you have more replicates than in your previous models; space-time  models can quickly become very very large…
Finn

but not:

          bru_obs(

            family = "gaussian",

              prec = list(initial = 4, fixed = TRUE)))
          )

Can you please explain the difference between the two?

On Wednesday, December 18, 2024 at 7:49:05 PM UTC+13 Finn Lindgren wrote:
> That model doesn’t have any covariates, just two scalar variables x1 and x2.
> Since those are by default model=“linear”, you can set their prior mean and precision with
>
> comp <- 0+x1(1, mean.linear=…, prec.linear=…) + x2(…1)
>
> But since the predictor expression will also become a scalar, you may still need to use the rep(1, nrow(.data.)) as input to x1 and x2 to help inlabru figure out the appropriate size of the predictor.
>
> Btw, I assume you meant exp(x1) + x1 * x2 in the predictor.
>
> Finn
>
> > On 18 Dec 2024, at 00:26, Louis Li <cooki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > ﻿
> > Thank you for your answer, but I have probably asked incorrectly, and currently it seems to work with:
> >
> > formula <- y ~ exp(x1) + x1x2
> > comp <- ~ 0 + x1(1) + x2(1)
> > fit <- bru(comp, bru_obs(formula, family="gaussian", data=data))
> >
> > But now I'm facing a new problem. How do I specify priors on x1 and x2? I'm guessing it would involve using two linear components, but I couldn't find such an example of using multiple components.
> >
> >
> > On Tuesday, December 17, 2024 at 9:10:46 PM UTC+13 Finn Lindgren wrote:
> > > Hi Louis,
> > >
> > > this is where linear model shorthand breaks down a bit, as it
> > > conflates the values of a covariate with the _effect_ of the
> > > covariate.
> > > I _think_ what you want is the following model:
> > >
> > > y[i] ~ exp(beta1*x1[i]) + beta2 * (x1[i] * x2[i])
> > >
> > > where x1 and x2 are known numerical vectors where beta1 and beta2 are
> > > unknown coefficients with Gaussian priors, and
> > >
> > > y[i] ~ exp(beta1*x1[i]) + sum_k beta2[k] * x12[k]
> > >
> > > if x2 is a factor variable, and x12 is whatever model.matrix()
> > > constructs for the x1:x2 notation.
> > >
> > > Then you can write this model with inlabru, in several ways:
> > >
> > > Option 1, combined component effects:
> > > comp <- ~ 0 + x1(x1) + x12(~ 0 + x1:x2, model = "fixed")
> > > formula <- y ~ exp(x1) + x12
> > > fit <- bru(comp, bru_obs(formula, data = data.frame(x1=...,x2=...,y=...)))
> > >
> > > In the predictor formula, x1 and x12 are the _effects of_ the
> > > component definitions, i.e. beta1*x1[i] etc.
> > > This also works if x1 or x2 are factor variables.
> > > If both are numeric, the x12 component can be written x12(x1*x2) instead.
> > >
> > > Option 2, explicit variables:
> > > comp <- ~ 0 + beta1(rep(1, nrow(.data.))) + beta2(rep(1, nrow(.data.)))
> > > formula <- y ~ exp(beta1 * x1) + beta2 * x1 *x2
> > > fit <- bru(comp, bru_obs(formula, data = data.frame(x1=...,x2=...,y=...)))
> > >
> > > (in the case x1 and x2 are numeric covariates)
> > >
> > > In your case, I'd probably go with Option 1.
> > >
> > > If you don't have the latest inlabru, use like() instead of bru_obs().
> > >
> > > Finn
> > >
> > > On Tue, 17 Dec 2024 at 04:44, Louis Li <cooki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Dear INLA experts,
> > > >
> > > > Suppose I have covariates x1, x2 (gaussian priors) and a model y ~ exp(x1) + x1:x2, and I want the marginal posterior densities of x1 and x2.
> > > >
> > > > Is it possible to do in INLA or inlabru? Also how can I make R keep the coefficients of these two terms as 1, and have R recognize x1 and x2 as covariates instead of exp(x1) and x1:x2?
> > > >
> > > > Thanks in advance.
> > > > Louis

messages.subject: Convergence issues: The Newton-Raphson optimizer did not converge
messages.subject_clean: Convergence issues: The Newton-Raphson optimizer did not converge
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community,

I run a zero-inflated negative binomial AR1 model with spatial fields and temporal structure. On subsets of the data, I manage to run it on HPC, but full datasets fail to converge:

inla: tabulate-Qfunc.c:147: GMRFLib_tabulate_Qfunc_core: Assertion `arg->Q->a[0] >= 0.0' failed.
sh: line 1: 4090757 Segmentation fault      (core dumped) '/apps/gent/RHEL8/zen3x-ib/software/R-INLA/24.01.18-foss-2023a/INLA/bin/linux/64bit/inla.run' -s -v -t8:1 -P compact '/tmp/RtmpzG8dj4/file3e6a0444a7c77e/Model.ini' > '/tmp/RtmpzG8dj4/file3e6a0444a7c77e/Logfile.txt'
GMRFLib_2order_approx: rescue NAN/INF values in logl for idx=0
GMRFLib_2order_approx: rescue NAN/INF values in logl for idx=1
GMRFLib_2order_approx: rescue NAN/INF values in logl for idx=2
(...)
Reason    : The Newton-Raphson optimizer did not converge
Message   : Condition `lambda < 1.0 / lambda_lim' is not TRUE
Function  : GMRFLib_init_GMRF_approximation_store__intern

I have found literature on scaling issues with the data and/or the temporal variability of the mesh structure, but I struggle to find a solution so far.

This is my mesh:
max_edge = c(5, 10e5) # in meters
  Loc = cbind(strandline70$X, strandline70$Y)
  mesh = inla.mesh.2d(boundary = beaches,
                      loc = Loc,
                      max.edge = max_edge,
                      cutoff = 5,
                      offset = c(10e3,10e2))

My data set contains abundances from 1-2000 individuals as the response variable.

Can anyone help me?

Kind regards,

Charlotte Taelman

messages.body_plain:
The spatial units, m or km, need to be chosen according to the size/scale of the modelling region. Metres can be fine for small regions. For larger scales, transforming to km is needed to avoid nunerical precision issues.

If all data have crs info, and a crs with km units is supplied to fm_mesh_2d, then the make.A functions etc can automatically map the data to the mesh.
If one want more control over that, use fm_transform() to convert the data to the km crs first.

crskm<- crs
fm_length_unit(crskm) <- "km"

Finn
